statement.essentials: After injury, the nerve fibres that should make saliva can grow into the sweat glands of the skin, so that eating makes the skin over the gland sweat.
statement.anatomy: Frey syndrome, sweating when eating, is thought to result from abnormal reinnervation after injury to the auriculotemporal nerve: its parasympathetic fibres normally stimulate saliva and its sympathetic fibres supply the sweat glands of the face and scalp.
statement.clinical: Frey syndrome is a recognised complication of parotid surgery; one review reports tumour size and mass volume as the only statistically significant predictors. A thicker skin flap, or a barrier such as a SMAS or temporoparietal fascia flap, has been used to prevent it.

limitations: The reinnervation explanation is the accepted mechanism rather than something observed in individual patients; the regrowth drawn in the model is a schematic of that idea, not a measured structure. Predictors come from one review’s account of a single series.
